readings.title: Comparing the price of a phone plan
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community class compared monthly phone plans. Participants noticed that the cheapest advertised price did not always mean the lowest yearly cost. The main obstacle was extra charges outside the headline price. Some plans charged for basic data after a small allowance was used. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a twelve-month cost comparison. Learners added regular fees and likely usage costs for two different households. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated total cost depended on realistic use. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a comparison sheet showing typical yearly totals. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: price decisions require a common measure. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in comparing the price of a phone plan, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Planning for an irregular bill
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Several households could meet normal weekly costs but struggled when a yearly insurance bill arrived in one month. The main obstacle was a large bill missing from weekly plans. People had treated predictable annual costs as if they were unexpected emergencies. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a calendar of recurring payments. Advisers helped families list dates without asking them to disclose private account details. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated small regular savings could cover known costs. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a separate monthly reserve for yearly bills. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: a budget should include the whole year. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in planning for an irregular bill, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A misleading online discount
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Shoppers at a digital-skills workshop examined a sale page. Its large discount appeared attractive until delivery costs were added. The main obstacle was a displayed saving that hid the final amount. The offer also required buying two items, although many people needed only one. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a comparison of complete checkout prices. Participants recorded quantities, delivery charges and conditions before comparing offers. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated the discount was poor value for single buyers. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a checklist for full prices and purchase conditions. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: an offer is useful only in context. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a misleading online discount, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Explaining a loan repayment table
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A credit advice office gave visitors a repayment table. Some readers focused on the first instalment and overlooked the total paid. The main obstacle was attention fixed on one monthly figure. A longer loan made each payment smaller while increasing the overall amount. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a visual comparison of repayment periods. Advisers showed identical loan amounts over different terms with clear total-cost columns. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated payment size alone was not enough to judge a loan. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a summary line for total repayment and duration. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: financial choices need both short and long views. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in explaining a loan repayment table, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning household budgets and financial literacy often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the household money advice programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有关家庭预算与金融素养的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the money advice team proposing a small improvement to the household money advice programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the household money advice programme. People have noticed extra charges outside the headline price, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
